summary: A transfer function is the Laplace-domain ratio of output to input with zero initial conditions. You derive the transfer function of a DC motor from its two ODEs, build a small TF class with series and feedback connections, and close a speed loop around the motor.
html:
Definition

Take a linear ODE relating an input u to an output y, transform it with all initial conditions zero, and divide:

G(s)=U(s)Y(s)​=an​sn+⋯+a0​bm​sm+⋯+b0​​.

For a2​y¨​+a1​y˙​+a0​y=b0​u that’s G(s)=b0​/(a2​s2+a1​s+a0​): the denominator is the characteristic polynomial from Phase 02, and its roots are the system’s poles.

Three numbers you can read off without solving anything:

  • DC gain G(0)=b0​/a0​: the steady output per unit of constant input.
  • Poles: roots of the denominator; they set the natural responses ept.
  • Frequency response G(jω): the phasor gain at frequency ω (lesson 9 of Phase 05).

The DC motor

The armature circuit and the rotor give two coupled equations, with voltage V, current i and speed ω:

Ldtdi​=V−Ri−Kω,Jdtdω​=Ki−bω.

K is both the torque constant (N·m/A) and the back-EMF constant (V·s/rad); in SI units they’re equal because the motor conserves energy. Transform with zero initial conditions:

(Ls+R)I=V−KΩ,(Js+b)Ω=KI.

Eliminate I=(Js+b)Ω/K:

G(s)=V(s)Ω(s)​=(Js+b)(Ls+R)+K2K​.

The K2 term is the back-EMF loop: faster rotation generates a voltage that opposes the supply.

Block algebra

Blocks in series multiply: G2​G1​. A feedback loop with forward path G and sensor H (negative feedback) gives

T(s)=1+GHG​.

Derivation: the error is E=R−HY and Y=GE, so Y=G(R−HY), which rearranges to Y(1+GH)=GR. With polynomials G=nG​/dG​ and H=nH​/dH​:

T=dG​dH​+nG​nH​nG​dH​​.

So every block diagram reduces to polynomial products and sums.

Worked example

A small brushed motor has J=10−4 kg·m², b=10−5 N·m·s, K=0.05 N·m/A, R=1 Ω and L=1 mH.

  1. Denominator: JLs2+(JR+bL)s+(bR+K2)=10−7s2+1.0001×10−4s+2.51×10−3.
  2. Poles: s=−974.3 and s=−25.76 s⁻¹. The fast one, with a 1.03 ms time constant, is electrical; the slow one, at 38.8 ms, is mechanical.
  3. DC gain: K/(bR+K2)=0.05/0.00251=19.92 rad/s per volt. At 12 V the motor spins at 239 rad/s (2283 rpm).
  4. Close a proportional speed loop with Kp​=0.5 V per rad/s and unity sensor H=1. The closed-loop denominator becomes 10−7s2+1.0001×10−4s+0.02751.
  5. Closed-loop poles: −500.05±158.27j s⁻¹, so ωn​=524.5 rad/s and ζ=0.953. The response is about 20 times faster than open loop.
  6. Closed-loop DC gain: 0.5×0.05/0.02751=0.9088. A proportional loop leaves a 9.1 % steady-state error; lesson 7 predicts it without simulating, and integral action in Phase 13 removes it.

Code it from scratch

tf.py
import numpy as np

class TF:
    """Transfer function as numerator/denominator coefficient arrays (highest power first)."""
    def __init__(self, num, den):
        self.num = np.trim_zeros(np.atleast_1d(np.asarray(num, float)), "f")
        self.den = np.trim_zeros(np.atleast_1d(np.asarray(den, float)), "f")

    def __mul__(self, o):            # series
        return TF(np.polymul(self.num, o.num), np.polymul(self.den, o.den))

    def feedback(self, H=None):      # negative feedback, unity by default
        H = H or TF([1], [1])
        return TF(np.polymul(self.num, H.den),
                  np.polyadd(np.polymul(self.den, H.den), np.polymul(self.num, H.num)))

    def __call__(self, s):
        return np.polyval(self.num, s) / np.polyval(self.den, s)

    poles = property(lambda self: np.roots(self.den))
    dc = property(lambda self: self(0.0))

def motor(J=1e-4, b=1e-5, K=0.05, R=1.0, L=1e-3):
    return TF([K], np.polyadd(np.polymul([J, b], [L, R]), [K * K]))

if __name__ == "__main__":
    G = motor()
    print("open-loop poles", np.round(np.sort(G.poles.real), 2), "DC gain", round(G.dc, 3))
    assert np.allclose(np.sort(G.poles.real), [-974.3389, -25.7611], atol=1e-3)
    assert abs(G.dc - 19.9203) < 1e-3
    T = (TF([0.5], [1]) * G).feedback()
    p = T.poles
    assert np.allclose(sorted(p, key=lambda z: z.imag), [-500.05 - 158.2719j, -500.05 + 158.2719j], atol=1e-3)
    assert abs(T.dc - 0.90876) < 1e-4
    # feedback formula agrees with direct evaluation G/(1+G) at many frequencies
    w = np.logspace(0, 5, 200) * 1j
    Gc = 0.5 * G(w)
    assert np.allclose(T(w), Gc / (1 + Gc), rtol=1e-10)
    print("closed-loop poles", np.round(p, 2), "DC gain", round(T.dc, 4))

Exercises

A spring-mass-damper has mx¨+cx˙+kx=F. Write X(s)/F(s) and its DC gain.

Show the solution

G(s)=ms2+cs+k1​ and G(0)=1/k: a constant force F deflects the spring by F/k, as statics says.

Ignore the inductance (L=0) in the motor model. What does G(s) become, and what is the mechanical time constant with the numbers above?

Show the solution

G(s)=(Js+b)R+K2K​=τs+1K/(bR+K2)​ with τ=bR+K2JR​=0.0025110−4​=39.8 ms. That’s close to the 38.8 ms slow pole of the full model: dropping a fast pole barely moves the slow one.

Quiz

quiz.q: What is the DC gain of the example motor in rad/s per volt?
quiz.explain: K/(bR+K2)=0.05/0.00251.

quiz.q: What is the closed-loop DC gain with Kp​=0.5 and unity feedback?
quiz.explain: Kp​G(0)/(1+Kp​G(0)).

quiz.q: Negative feedback with forward path G and sensor H gives…
quiz.explain: From Y=G(R−HY).
options: G/(1−GH)
G/(1+GH)
GH/(1+G)
G+H

quiz.q: Which magnitude in s⁻¹ is the slow (mechanical) pole of the example motor?
quiz.explain: Roots of 10−7s2+1.0001×10−4s+2.51×10−3.
The output of one is the input of the next, so Y=G2​G1​U.

quiz.q: What is the DC gain of 1/(ms2+cs+k) for k=400 N/m, in metres per newton?
quiz.explain: G(0)=1/k.
